subtopic_detail: Tender concentric subareolar breast tissue in a pubertal boy with symmetrical testes and normal pubertal progression
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 14 year old boy brought in by his father because both his breasts have become swollen and sore over the past six months. He has stopped swimming with his friends and keeps his shirt on at the beach, and his father wants to know whether an operation is needed.

He takes no medication, uses no protein powders or muscle building supplements, and does not use cannabis or alcohol. He has grown 8 cm in the past year and his voice has begun to deepen.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21 kg/m2, a firm mobile tender disc of tissue about 3 cm across lying concentrically beneath each areola, no nipple discharge or skin tethering, no axillary lymphadenopathy, Tanner stage 3 pubic hair with testicular volume 10 mL on both sides and no testicular mass, no hepatomegaly, visual fields full to confrontation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Measure beta human chorionic gonadotrophin, testosterone and oestradiol today
options.rationale: A hormonal workup is indicated when the presentation is atypical, meaning onset before puberty, tissue larger than 4 cm, rapid growth, asymmetrical or hard tissue, or any testicular abnormality, since a human chorionic gonadotrophin secreting tumour is the finding that must not be missed. Symmetrical concentric tissue with equal normal testes in a boy at the expected pubertal stage does not meet any of those criteria. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Gynaecomastia in adolescence)
source_refs: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Gynaecomastia in adolescence

options.text: Refer to a paediatric surgeon for bilateral subcutaneous mastectomy of the tissue
options.rationale: Surgery is offered for persistent tissue causing significant distress after two to three years, by which time spontaneous resolution has clearly failed. Operating during active puberty risks recurrence as the hormonal imbalance continues, and carries scarring and nipple sensory loss. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Gynaecomastia in adolescence)
source_refs: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Gynaecomastia in adolescence

options.text: Reassure with an explanation of the natural history and review him in six months
options.rationale: Breast tissue develops in up to two thirds of boys during mid puberty because testicular oestradiol production rises before testosterone does, and it resolves spontaneously within about two years in the great majority. Symmetrical tender concentric tissue with normally progressing puberty and equal testes is the physiological pattern, so explanation and planned review is the management. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Gynaecomastia in adolescence)
source_refs: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Gynaecomastia in adolescence

options.text: Commence tamoxifen to reduce the glandular tissue over the next three months
options.rationale: Tamoxifen has been shown to reduce breast volume and tenderness in adolescents and is sometimes used for painful tissue that persists, though it is not registered for this purpose in Australia. It is reserved for persistent or markedly symptomatic cases rather than offered before the natural history has been allowed to run. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Tamoxifen)

options.text: Arrange a scrotal ultrasound scan and a karyotype to look for a syndromic cause
options.rationale: Scrotal imaging is indicated when a testis is asymmetrical or a mass is felt, and a karyotype is arranged when the testes are small and firm with tall stature and learning difficulties, which suggests Klinefelter syndrome. His testicular volumes are equal and appropriate for his pubertal stage with no mass, so neither test is indicated. (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Gynaecomastia in adolescence)
source_refs: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Gynaecomastia in adolescence

explanation.summary: Pubertal gynaecomastia is a physiological phenomenon affecting up to around two thirds of adolescent boys, peaking at Tanner stages 3 and 4, and arises because testicular oestradiol secretion and peripheral aromatisation rise earlier in puberty than testosterone production does. The tissue is typically tender, symmetrical or nearly so, and lies concentrically beneath the areola, which separates it from the soft diffuse fat of pseudogynaecomastia in an overweight boy and from the hard eccentric fixed mass of the very rare adolescent breast malignancy. Resolution occurs within about two years in the large majority, so explanation and review are usually all that is required, and acknowledging the psychological impact matters because distress and social avoidance are common. Investigation is reserved for atypical features, and the differential then includes human chorionic gonadotrophin secreting germ cell tumours, Klinefelter syndrome, liver and thyroid disease, and drugs, with spironolactone, cimetidine, ketoconazole, antipsychotics, anabolic steroids and cannabis among the commoner causes. Tamoxifen is used for persistent painful tissue and surgery for tissue that has not resolved after two to three years and continues to cause distress.
key_points: It affects up to two thirds of boys and peaks at Tanner stages 3 and 4
Tissue is tender, concentric beneath the areola and largely symmetrical
The great majority resolve spontaneously within about two years
Investigate for prepubertal onset, tissue over 4 cm, rapid growth or a testicular mass
Ask specifically about anabolic steroids, cannabis, spironolactone and antipsychotics
explanation.pearls: Palpate both testes at the same visit rather than examining the chest alone: a unilateral testicular mass with gynaecomastia signals a human chorionic gonadotrophin secreting germ cell tumour, and the breast tissue is frequently the symptom that brings the boy in while the testicular lump has gone unnoticed.

sources.label: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Gynaecomastia in adolescence
Australian Medicines Handbook: Tamoxifen
BMJ Best Practice: Gynaecomastia

subtopic_detail: Inward pointing feet in a toddler with normal hip rotation and an inwardly rotated thigh foot axis
stem:
You are the registrar in a general paediatric clinic reviewing a 2 year old girl whose parents say both her feet point inwards when she walks and that she trips over more than other children at her playgroup. They have been told by a relative that she needs special boots before the bones set.

She walked at 13 months, has no pain, and keeps up with her older brother in the park. She sits on the floor with her legs out in front rather than between her heels.

data_table.Examination: Feet point inwards symmetrically during gait, hip internal rotation 45 degrees and external rotation 45 degrees bilaterally in the prone position, thigh foot axis 20 degrees internal on both sides, forefoot border straight, no leg length difference and full painless knee and ankle movement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the parents and review her gait at the next routine visit
options.rationale: Symmetrical hip rotation excludes femoral anteversion and a straight forefoot border excludes metatarsus adductus, localising the rotation to the tibia, and an internal thigh foot axis at this age is the expected finding. Internal tibial torsion unwinds with normal growth and resolves in nearly all children by about eight years without any intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations

options.text: Prescribe a night time derotation brace to be worn until school age
options.rationale: Derotation bracing and twister cables were historically used for this exact presentation but randomised comparison showed no change in the rate of correction over untreated children, and they disturb sleep for years. This is the anti-pattern the family has already been offered by a relative. (Source: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations

options.text: Request standing radiographs of both lower limbs to measure the torsion
options.rationale: Plain films measure angular deformity in the coronal plane but cannot quantify rotation, which is a torsional profile measured clinically at the hip, tibia and foot. Imaging a child whose rotational profile is already normal for age adds radiation without changing management. (Source: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for consideration of a tibial derotation osteotomy
options.rationale: Osteotomy is reserved for a thigh foot axis beyond about 30 degrees that persists past eight to ten years with functional disability, by which age spontaneous correction has clearly failed. Operating on a 2 year old within the normal range would be surgery for a variant that is going to resolve. (Source: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations

options.text: Advise she avoid sitting in the W position and start corrective footwear
options.rationale: Discouraging W sitting is directed at femoral anteversion, and this child already sits with her legs in front of her, so the advice addresses a mechanism she does not have. Corrective or wedged footwear has never been shown to alter torsional alignment at any level. (Source: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations

explanation.summary: Intoeing is assessed by working down the rotational profile rather than by looking at the feet, because the three causes sit at three different levels and have different natural histories. Metatarsus adductus arises in the foot and is recognised by a curved lateral forefoot border, usually resolving in infancy. Internal tibial torsion arises in the tibia, is measured by the thigh foot axis, peaks in the second year and unwinds by school age. Femoral anteversion arises at the hip, is recognised by internal rotation well exceeding external rotation in the prone position, presents later at four to six years and also corrects spontaneously in the great majority. Referral is reserved for asymmetry, pain, progression after age eight, or a functionally disabling rotational profile.
key_points: Work down the rotational profile: hip rotation, thigh foot axis, then forefoot border
Symmetrical hip rotation with an internal thigh foot axis localises the cause to the tibia
Internal tibial torsion peaks in the second year and resolves by around eight years
Braces, twister cables and corrective footwear do not alter torsional correction
Asymmetry, pain or progression after eight years are the triggers for referral
explanation.pearls: Measure the thigh foot axis with the child prone and the knee flexed to 90 degrees: values between 10 degrees internal and 15 degrees external are normal at two years, and only persistence beyond 30 degrees internal after eight years has ever justified surgery.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Intoeing and gait variations
Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric lower limb variants
BMJ Best Practice: Intoeing in children

subtopic_detail: Bowed legs and wrist swelling in a prolonged breastfed toddler with a raised alkaline phosphatase and symmetrical metaphyseal change
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing an 18 month old girl referred because her legs have become increasingly bowed since she started walking at 16 months. Her mother says her wrists look knobbly and that she is slower to get up off the floor than her cousin of the same age.

She was breastfed as her only milk until 14 months and now drinks small amounts of cow's milk. Her mother has deeply pigmented skin, wears clothing covering her arms and legs outdoors, and takes no supplements. There are no bruises anywhere on the child, and the family has no history of bone disease or fractures.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical genu varum, widened painless wrists and costochondral junctions, anterior fontanelle closed, no bruising or skin injury, normal tone and power
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.12 mmol/L (2.20-2.65), phosphate 0.85 mmol/L (1.20-1.80), alkaline phosphatase 1180 U/L (110-320), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 14 nmol/L (greater than 50), parathyroid hormone elevated, urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, wrist radiograph shows symmetrical metaphyseal cupping and fraying at both distal radii

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Start oral calcitriol and repeat the calcium in two weeks
options.rationale: Calcitriol bypasses renal 1 alpha hydroxylation and is used in renal rickets or in vitamin D dependent rickets type 1, where that hydroxylation step is the problem. This child has normal renal function with a low 25 hydroxyvitamin D, so the deficient substrate is the native vitamin, not the active metabolite. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for bracing of the lower limb deformity
options.rationale: The bowing here is the mechanical consequence of unmineralised growth plate rather than a primary structural deformity, and it remodels once mineralisation is restored. Bracing an actively rachitic limb treats the visible endpoint while leaving the metabolic cause running. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

options.text: Give intravenous calcium gluconate and admit for cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Intravenous calcium is reserved for symptomatic hypocalcaemia with tetany, seizures or a prolonged QT interval, none of which is present with a calcium of 2.12 mmol/L. Correcting calcium alone also leaves the vitamin D deficit that is driving secondary hyperparathyroidism. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

options.text: Arrange a skeletal survey and notify child protection services
options.rationale: Metaphyseal irregularity does raise the question of inflicted injury, but the classic metaphyseal lesion of abuse is a corner or bucket handle fracture rather than symmetrical cupping and fraying, and it is not accompanied by a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase with a low 25 hydroxyvitamin D. The biochemical picture explains the radiology without a second mechanism. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Start oral cholecalciferol with supplemental dietary calcium
options.rationale: Nutritional rickets from maternal and infant vitamin D deficiency is corrected by replacing the deficient substrate as cholecalciferol, and calcium intake is increased at the same time because remineralising bone consumes calcium rapidly once treatment starts. Alkaline phosphatase and radiographic healing are used to confirm response over the following months. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

explanation.summary: Nutritional rickets in Australia clusters in children of mothers with deeply pigmented skin or extensive sun avoidance who are breastfed beyond twelve months without supplementation, because breast milk contains very little vitamin D and the infant's stores reflect the mother's status. The biochemical signature is a low or low normal calcium with a low phosphate, a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase and secondary hyperparathyroidism, with radiographs showing metaphyseal cupping, fraying and splaying at the fastest growing physes. Treatment replaces cholecalciferol and ensures adequate calcium, since hungry bone during healing can otherwise drop the calcium further. The mother and any siblings should be tested, because the deficiency is a household exposure rather than an isolated event. Untreated disease produces permanent limb deformity, delayed motor milestones and hypocalcaemic seizures.
key_points: Breast milk alone beyond twelve months without supplementation is the usual Australian setting
Low phosphate with a very high alkaline phosphatase and raised parathyroid hormone is the signature
Symmetrical metaphyseal cupping and fraying distinguishes rickets from inflicted metaphyseal injury
Calcium is supplemented alongside cholecalciferol because healing bone consumes it
Test the mother and siblings, since the exposure is shared
explanation.pearls: Recheck the alkaline phosphatase at four weeks rather than the vitamin D level: a falling alkaline phosphatase confirms the bone is remineralising, whereas the 25 hydroxyvitamin D rises within days of the first dose and says nothing about whether the rickets is healing.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency
RCH CPG: Child abuse
Australian and New Zealand Bone and Mineral Society: Vitamin D and health position statement

subtopic_detail: Repeated nosebleeds from one nostril in a school aged child with normal platelets and normal coagulation
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6 year old boy brought in because he has had nosebleeds most weeks through the winter. His mother says blood comes from the right side only, it stops within about five minutes when she pinches the soft part of his nose, and it usually happens after he has been picking at it.

He has eczema treated with a moisturiser and uses no other medications. He has never bled from his gums or had bleeding after a dental extraction, and no one in the family bruises easily or has needed treatment for bleeding.

data_table.Examination: Prominent dilated vessels on the anterior right nasal septum with a small area of adherent crust, no septal perforation, no facial or oral petechiae, no bruising or lymphadenopathy, spleen not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 124 g/L (115-155), platelets 286 x10^9/L (150-400), white cell count within normal limits, prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to an ear nose and throat surgeon for examination under anaesthesia
options.rationale: Examination under anaesthesia is for bleeding that is posterior, unable to be controlled, or suspicious for a mass such as juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma in an adolescent boy with obstruction. An anterior septal source that is directly visible and stops with five minutes of pressure does not need theatre. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

options.text: Apply an antiseptic nasal cream to the affected nostril for two weeks
options.rationale: Recurrent anterior bleeding in a child comes from dilated vessels on Little's area kept raw by crusting, digital trauma and dry air, and an antiseptic cream reduces colonisation and keeps the mucosa moist so the vessels re epithelialise. It outperforms cautery for first line use in children and avoids the discomfort and septal risk of a chemical burn. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

options.text: Cauterise the bleeding point with a silver nitrate stick at this visit
options.rationale: Silver nitrate cautery is second line in children once topical treatment has failed, because it is painful without topical anaesthesia and causes further crusting that can restart the cycle. Cautery is also never applied to both sides of the septum at one sitting given the risk of perforation. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

options.text: Request von Willebrand factor assays and a platelet function analysis
options.rationale: A bleeding disorder workup is triggered by bleeding from both nostrils, bleeding lasting beyond ten to twenty minutes despite pressure, mucosal bleeding at other sites, a positive family history or an abnormal screening count. This child has a normal platelet count, a normal coagulation screen and none of those features. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

options.text: Prescribe oral tranexamic acid to be taken through the winter months
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid has a role in heavy or recurrent bleeding in patients with a diagnosed bleeding disorder or in acute uncontrolled epistaxis, not as seasonal prophylaxis in a child with a visible local lesion. Systemic antifibrinolysis does not address the mucosal breakdown that is generating the bleeding. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Tranexamic acid)

explanation.summary: Almost all childhood epistaxis is anterior and arises from Kiesselbach's plexus on the cartilaginous septum, where a superficial vascular network sits immediately under thin mucosa. The cycle is crusting, picking, bleeding and recrusting, which is why treatment aims at mucosal healing rather than at the vessel itself. First aid taught to families is ten minutes of continuous pressure on the soft part of the nose with the child leaning forwards, not pinching the bony bridge or tipping the head back. Investigation is reserved for bleeding that is bilateral, prolonged despite correct pressure, accompanied by bleeding elsewhere, or associated with an abnormal blood count. Persistent unilateral bleeding with nasal obstruction in an adolescent boy is the one presentation that mandates urgent imaging and specialist review.
key_points: Anterior septal vessels on Little's area are the source in the great majority of children
Antiseptic nasal cream is first line and outperforms cautery in children
Correct first aid is ten minutes of pressure on the soft nose while leaning forwards
Bilateral or prolonged bleeding or bleeding at other sites triggers a haematology workup
Unilateral bleeding with obstruction in an adolescent boy needs imaging for angiofibroma
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the child bled for more than twenty minutes despite correct pressure, or bled after tonsillectomy or dental extraction: those two answers, not the frequency of nosebleeds, are what separate a local septal lesion from undiagnosed von Willebrand disease.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Epistaxis
Australian Medicines Handbook: Tranexamic acid
BMJ Best Practice: Epistaxis in children

subtopic_detail: Midline translucent membrane fusing the labia minora in a preschool girl who voids normally
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 3 year old girl whose mother noticed while bathing her that the opening between her lips looks closed over and is worried that she has been born with something missing.

The child is toilet trained, passes a normal stream without straining or dribbling afterwards, and has never had a urinary infection or a fever without a cause. She has no itch, no discharge and no pain, and her mother has not seen her scratching or touching the area.

data_table.Examination: Labia minora fused in the midline by a thin translucent membrane with a visible pale line along the fusion, a patent opening anteriorly through which the urethral meatus is seen, vulval skin otherwise normal with no erythema, excoriation, whitening or bruising
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for leucocytes, nitrites and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply a topical oestrogen cream along the fusion line each night
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen is reserved for adhesions causing urinary symptoms such as post void dribbling, recurrent infection or voiding difficulty, since it commonly produces local irritation, breast budding and vaginal bleeding on withdrawal. Treating an asymptomatic child accepts those effects for no clinical gain. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

options.text: Separate the adhesion manually during this consultation
options.rationale: Forcible separation tears the epithelium, is painful and frightening for a preschool child, and leaves raw opposed surfaces that refuse at a higher rate than before. Separation under topical anaesthesia belongs only to symptomatic adhesions that have failed medical treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

options.text: Refer for surgical division of the adhesion under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Surgical division is limited to dense adhesions with urinary retention or recurrent infection that have not responded to topical treatment, and recurrence is common while oestrogen levels remain low. This is an operation for a finding that resolves by itself at puberty. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

options.text: Reassure the parents and review at the next scheduled health check
options.rationale: Asymptomatic labial adhesions occur in oestrogen deficient vulval skin between about three months and six years, and they separate spontaneously as endogenous oestrogen rises at puberty if not before. Normal voiding with a visible urethral meatus and no infection confirms there is nothing to treat, so the intervention is explanation and simple vulval care. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

options.text: Apply a topical betamethasone ointment along the fusion line nightly
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid is an alternative to oestrogen for symptomatic adhesions and is the treatment of choice for the white atrophic plaques of lichen sclerosus, which this child does not have. Steroid on normal vulval skin in an asymptomatic child risks local atrophy without addressing a problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

explanation.summary: Labial adhesions are an acquired fusion of the labia minora in the low oestrogen years of childhood, typically appearing between three months and six years, and are frequently mistaken by families for an absent or abnormal vaginal opening. The membrane is thin, translucent and midline, with a visible pale raphe, which distinguishes it from the thickened white atrophic skin of lichen sclerosus and from congenital anomalies where no separate structures are identifiable. Management is determined entirely by symptoms, and the asymptomatic child needs explanation, avoidance of soaps and bubble baths, and review. Treatment with topical oestrogen or corticosteroid is offered for post void dribbling, recurrent urinary infection or voiding obstruction, and recurrence after any treatment is common until puberty. Vulval bruising, bleeding, or an adhesion with genital injury requires assessment for sexual abuse.
key_points: A thin translucent midline membrane with a pale raphe is diagnostic on inspection
Adhesions arise in the low oestrogen years and resolve as puberty approaches
Symptoms, not appearance, determine whether any treatment is offered
Topical oestrogen or corticosteroid is for dribbling, infection or obstruction only
White atrophic plaques with fissuring indicate lichen sclerosus instead
explanation.pearls: Ask whether urine dribbles out when she stands up after voiding: that single symptom, caused by urine pooling behind the fusion, is the usual indication that turns an observed adhesion into one worth treating with topical oestrogen.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Paediatric and adolescent gynaecology
BMJ Best Practice: Labial adhesions

subtopic_detail: Ballooning of the foreskin on voiding in a preschool boy with a healthy pink preputial opening
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 4 year old boy whose father has asked for a referral for circumcision. He says the foreskin puffs up like a balloon when the boy passes urine and then the urine comes out in a normal stream, and that the foreskin has never pulled back.

The boy has had no urinary infections, no fevers without a cause and no pain when he passes urine. His father has been pulling the foreskin back a little each bath time because he was told it would loosen it.

data_table.Examination: Foreskin non retractile with a soft pink preputial opening that pouts on gentle traction, no white scarring or thickened ring at the tip, glans not visible, no erythema, discharge or tenderness of the prepuce
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for leucocytes and nitrites

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure about normal non retractility and advise against retraction
options.rationale: The prepuce is normally adherent to the glans in early childhood and separates spontaneously, with only about half of boys retractile at ten years and nearly all by the late teens, and ballooning is the normal consequence of urine passing into a preputial space that has not yet separated. Forced retraction tears the adhesions and creates the scarred ring that genuinely does require treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

options.text: Apply a topical corticosteroid ointment to the preputial tip for six weeks
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid is effective treatment for pathological phimosis, where a fibrotic white ring prevents retraction, and it resolves the majority of such cases without surgery. Applying it to a physiologically non retractile foreskin with a soft pink opening treats normal developmental anatomy. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

options.text: Refer to a paediatric surgeon for circumcision on the current waiting list
options.rationale: Medical indications for circumcision are pathological phimosis with scarring, recurrent balanoposthitis and recurrent urinary infection with an abnormal urinary tract, none of which is present. Ballooning alone has never been an indication for operation. (Source: RACP: Circumcision of infant males position statement)
source_refs: RACP: Circumcision of infant males position statement

options.text: Teach the father a graded daily retraction routine with a lubricant
options.rationale: Graded retraction is the very practice that produces microtears, bleeding and secondary cicatricial scarring at the preputial tip, converting a normal foreskin into one that is pathologically phimotic. The father is already doing this and needs to be asked to stop. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

options.text: Prescribe an oral antibiotic and arrange a renal tract ultrasound scan
options.rationale: Antibiotics and imaging follow a confirmed urinary tract infection, and this boy has no fever, no dysuria and a negative dipstick, so there is no infection to treat or to image. Ballooning does not indicate obstruction and does not raise the risk of infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Physiological phimosis is the normal state of the prepuce in childhood, where the inner preputial epithelium remains adherent to the glans and separates over years under the influence of intermittent erections and desquamation. Ballooning during voiding reflects urine entering that unseparated space and is not evidence of obstruction, provided the stream is normal and the child is comfortable. Pathological phimosis is a different entity, recognised by a white fibrotic ring at the preputial tip that does not pout on traction, and is usually caused either by forced retraction or by balanitis xerotica obliterans. It is treated first with a topical corticosteroid, which avoids surgery in most cases, with circumcision reserved for failure or for recurrent balanoposthitis. Preputial adhesions that are torn by retraction bleed, hurt, and heal with the scarring that later justifies the operation the family originally wanted.
key_points: Non retractility at four years is normal and roughly half of boys are retractile by ten
Ballooning with a normal stream indicates unseparated adhesions, not obstruction
A soft pink pouting preputial opening excludes pathological phimosis
Forced retraction causes the cicatricial scarring that creates true phimosis
Topical corticosteroid resolves most pathological phimosis without circumcision
explanation.pearls: Look for whether the preputial opening pouts outwards on gentle traction: a soft pink pout is physiological and needs no treatment, whereas a rigid white ring that stays contracted is balanitis xerotica obliterans and warrants a six week course of topical corticosteroid before any surgical referral.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Foreskin care
RACP: Circumcision of infant males position statement
RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection

subtopic_detail: Fevers recurring on a fixed monthly cycle with oral ulceration and a neutrophilia measured during an episode
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4 year old boy in clinic whose mother has kept a diary showing fevers to 39.5 degrees Celsius lasting four days and arriving every 26 to 28 days for the past eight months. She can predict the next episode to within two days.

During an episode he has a sore throat, sore spots inside his mouth and tender lumps in his neck, but no cough, coryza or rash. Between episodes he is entirely well, attends kindergarten without absence, and has tracked along the 50th centile for height and weight throughout. Three throat swabs taken during separate episodes have grown no group A streptococcus, and he has had no skin or deep tissue infections.

data_table.Vital signs: During today's episode: pulse 132 per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Two shallow aphthous ulcers on the buccal mucosa, injected pharynx with scant exudate, tender bilateral cervical nodes up to 2 cm, no hepatosplenomegaly, no rash or joint swelling
data_table.Investigations: Taken today during the episode: white cell count 15.6 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0) with neutrophils 11.2 x10^9/L (1.5-8.0), haemoglobin 121 g/L (115-155), platelets 342 x10^9/L (150-400), C reactive protein 68 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange full blood counts twice weekly over the next six weeks
options.rationale: Serial counts across a cycle are how cyclical neutropenia is diagnosed, since the nadir is transient and dated to a 21 day rhythm. That diagnosis is already excluded here because the count taken during fever shows a neutrophilia of 11.2 x10^9/L, whereas cyclical neutropenia produces fever precisely when the neutrophils are at their lowest. (Source: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes)

options.text: Refer for tonsillectomy as definitive treatment of the recurrent episodes
options.rationale: Tonsillectomy does abolish episodes in a substantial proportion of children with this syndrome and is a recognised option, but it is considered only after the diagnosis has been confirmed and when episodes remain disruptive despite medical treatment. Proceeding to surgery before a steroid response has been demonstrated removes the cheapest diagnostic and therapeutic step. (Source: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes)

options.text: Commence twice daily oral phenoxymethylpenicillin as long term prophylaxis
options.rationale: Antibiotic prophylaxis is directed at recurrent streptococcal pharyngitis, which would be supported by positive swabs during episodes and by a response to treatment. Three negative swabs during separate episodes, and fevers arriving on a fixed calendar rather than after exposures, place this outside a bacterial cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Send genetic testing for the Mediterranean fever gene before further treatment
options.rationale: Familial Mediterranean fever is the monogenic syndrome to consider, but its attacks are irregular rather than calendar predictable, last one to three days, and feature serositis with abdominal or chest pain and an erysipelas like rash rather than aphthous ulceration and adenitis. Testing is reserved for that phenotype or for a suggestive family origin and history. (Source: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes)

options.text: Give a single dose of oral prednisolone at the onset of the next episode
options.rationale: Periodic fever with aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis and adenitis is a clinical diagnosis resting on clockwork periodicity, complete wellness between episodes and normal growth, and a single corticosteroid dose aborts an episode within hours in a way no other cause of recurrent fever does. That response is therefore both the treatment and the strongest confirmation of the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes)

explanation.summary: Periodic fever with aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis and cervical adenitis is the commonest periodic fever syndrome of childhood, typically starting before five years of age and running a clockwork cycle of three to six weeks. The diagnosis is clinical and depends on three things that are all present here: rigid periodicity, complete wellbeing between attacks, and normal growth and development. Inflammatory markers rise steeply during episodes and normalise fully between them, which is why a count taken during fever is so informative. A single dose of corticosteroid aborts an attack within hours, although it may shorten the interval to the next episode, and families are counselled about that trade off. The syndrome resolves spontaneously over several years, and tonsillectomy is reserved for children whose episodes remain disruptive.
key_points: Clockwork periodicity with complete wellness between attacks defines the syndrome
Normal growth and development is required and its absence forces a wider workup
A neutrophilia during fever excludes cyclical neutropenia, where fever coincides with the nadir
A single corticosteroid dose aborts an episode within hours and supports the diagnosis
Steroid may shorten the interval to the next attack, which families should be told
explanation.pearls: Time the blood count to the febrile day rather than the well interval: a neutrophil count above 1.5 x10^9/L taken during fever excludes cyclical neutropenia in one test and saves six weeks of twice weekly venepuncture in a preschool child.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Periodic fever syndromes
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
BMJ Best Practice: Periodic fever syndromes

subtopic_detail: Painless limp of several weeks in a school aged boy with restricted hip abduction and normal inflammatory markers
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 7 year old boy whose parents say he has walked with a limp for about six weeks. He complains mostly of an ache in the front of his right thigh and in his knee after football training, and he has been reluctant to run at school.

He has had no fever, no night sweats and no weight loss, and no viral illness in the months before the limp began. He is otherwise well, takes no medication, and has never had a hip problem or a significant injury.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 per minute, blood pressure 102/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Antalgic gait on the right, right hip internal rotation 10 degrees compared with 40 degrees on the left, abduction restricted to 25 degrees, no groin or knee effusion, knee ligaments stable, no spinal tenderness and no rash
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 7.8 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), C reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 8 mm/h (less than 15)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.text: Ultrasound of the right hip with aspiration of any effusion identified
options.rationale: Ultrasound with aspiration is the pathway for suspected septic arthritis, where an effusion is drained and cultured urgently. With a temperature of 36.8 degrees Celsius, a C reactive protein of 3 mg/L and a six week history, none of the Kocher predictors is met and an aspiration would be an invasive test for a diagnosis already excluded. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: Plain radiographs of both hips including frog leg lateral projections
options.rationale: Weeks of painless limp with loss of internal rotation and abduction in a child of this age points to a structural problem of the femoral head, and plain films remain the first line test, with the frog leg lateral showing subchondral collapse that the anteroposterior view misses. Both hips are imaged because bilateral disease occurs in about one in ten children and changes the differential. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance detects marrow change before radiographic change and is the right test when films are normal but suspicion persists, or when the extent of head involvement must be staged. It is not the first imaging test in a child of this age, since it requires anaesthesia and plain films will usually answer the question. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: No imaging, with simple analgesia and clinical review in two weeks
options.rationale: Observation is reasonable for transient synovitis, which follows a viral illness, settles within one to two weeks and does not restrict abduction to this degree. A limp persisting for six weeks without a preceding illness has moved outside the window where watchful waiting is safe. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

options.text: Blood cultures with an urgent orthopaedic review for joint washout
options.rationale: Cultures and washout are the response to a febrile child with a hot irritable hip and raised inflammatory markers, where delay costs the joint. An afebrile child with normal inflammatory markers over six weeks does not have a surgical emergency. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)

explanation.summary: A limp in a school aged child is triaged first by whether it is acute and febrile, where septic arthritis and osteomyelitis dominate, or chronic and afebrile, where structural hip disease dominates. Legg Calve Perthes disease is idiopathic osteonecrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis, peaks between four and eight years, affects boys about four times as often, and presents with weeks of limp and referred thigh or knee pain rather than groin pain. The earliest and most reliable clinical sign is loss of internal rotation and abduction, which is why hip movement is examined in every child presenting with knee pain. Radiographs of both hips with a frog leg lateral are the first line investigation, and magnetic resonance is reserved for normal films with continuing suspicion. The key alternative diagnosis in an older or heavier child is a slipped upper femoral epiphysis, which shares referred knee pain and loss of internal rotation but demands immediate non weight bearing.
key_points: Knee pain in a child requires examination of the hip on the same side
Loss of internal rotation and abduction is the earliest sign of hip pathology
Perthes disease peaks at four to eight years and is four times commoner in boys
The frog leg lateral view shows subchondral collapse missed on the anteroposterior film
Normal inflammatory markers with weeks of symptoms exclude septic arthritis
explanation.pearls: Image both hips rather than the painful side alone: bilateral Perthes disease occurs in around ten per cent of children, and symmetrical involvement should prompt consideration of a skeletal dysplasia or hypothyroidism instead of idiopathic osteonecrosis.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Acute limp
Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric hip conditions
BMJ Best Practice: Legg Calve Perthes disease

subtopic_detail: Absent red reflex on one side in an infant whose family noticed a pale pupil in flash photographs
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 5 month old girl at her immunisation visit. Her mother shows you three photographs taken over the past two months in which the left pupil looks pale and creamy while the right pupil looks red, and says a friend told her it was just the camera.

The baby was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy, has no family history of eye disease or childhood cancer, and is feeding and growing normally. Her mother has noticed the left eye drifting outwards when she is tired.

data_table.Examination: Red reflex present on the right and absent on the left with a white reflex seen instead, left eye intermittently divergent on cover testing, both eyes of normal size with clear corneas, no proptosis, no orbital or lid swelling, no lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family that this is a photographic artefact and repeat the photographs
options.rationale: A camera artefact appears in both eyes on the same image and varies with the angle of the flash, whereas a consistently pale reflex on one side across separate photographs is the classic way retinoblastoma first comes to attention. The artefact explanation has already failed the test of reproducibility. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.text: Refer routinely for assessment of the divergent eye at twelve months of age
options.rationale: Routine referral is appropriate for a squint alone persisting beyond three months in an otherwise normal eye. Here the squint is secondary, because a tumour or opacity that destroys central vision causes the eye to drift, so treating it as an isolated strabismus would defer the urgent finding. (Source: RANZCO: Paediatric eye referral guidance)

options.text: Arrange an orbital ultrasound scan through the local radiology practice first
options.rationale: Ultrasound can demonstrate an intraocular mass with calcification and forms part of the specialist assessment, but arranging it independently inserts a delay of days to weeks before anyone with the means to examine the retina sees the child. Examination under anaesthesia with indirect ophthalmoscopy is what actually establishes the diagnosis and stages the eye. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.text: Refer to a paediatric ophthalmologist for assessment within the coming week
options.rationale: An absent red reflex in an infant carries a differential of retinoblastoma, congenital cataract, retinopathy of prematurity and Coats disease, and all of them are sight threatening or life threatening on a timescale of weeks. Direct specialist referral is therefore made on the clinical finding alone, without waiting for imaging or a second opinion. (Source: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria

options.text: Refer to a community optometrist for refraction and orthoptic assessment
options.rationale: Optometry and orthoptics manage refractive error and the amblyopia that follows a squint, and they cannot deliver the examination under anaesthesia and oncological staging this child may require. Referral to a service without that capability delays definitive assessment. (Source: RANZCO: Paediatric eye referral guidance)

explanation.summary: The red reflex test compares the reflection from both eyes simultaneously from about half a metre, and any asymmetry, dullness or white reflex is abnormal regardless of how well the infant appears to see. Retinoblastoma is the commonest intraocular malignancy of childhood, presents most often as leukocoria and second most often as a squint, and is diagnosed at a median age of around eighteen months for unilateral disease. Survival in Australia exceeds ninety five per cent when treatment is timely, so the outcome depends heavily on the interval between the first noticed abnormality and specialist assessment. Families very often report having seen the white pupil in photographs for months before presenting, having been reassured it was the camera. Every infant with an abnormal red reflex needs direct paediatric ophthalmology referral rather than investigation in primary care.
key_points: Compare both red reflexes simultaneously from about half a metre
Leukocoria and squint are the two commonest presentations of retinoblastoma
A reproducible pale pupil across separate photographs is not a camera artefact
A squint in an infant may be secondary to loss of central vision on that side
Refer directly to paediatric ophthalmology without arranging imaging first
explanation.pearls: Treat any squint appearing before three months, or any squint accompanied by an abnormal red reflex, as an urgent referral rather than a developmental variant, because a tumour that destroys central vision causes the eye to deviate and the squint is then the presenting sign of the cancer.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Red reflex and leukocoria
RANZCO: Paediatric eye referral guidance
Cancer Council Australia: Retinoblastoma

subtopic_detail: Restricted tongue elevation in a two week old with maternal nipple trauma and weight below birth weight
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 14 day old boy for a weight check. His mother describes cracked painful nipples that hurt through the whole feed, says he feeds for about an hour and wakes within thirty minutes wanting more, and has asked to be referred to have his tongue tie cut today.

She has had no fever, and there is no red wedge shaped area or lump in either breast. She has begun expressing after feeds and getting good volumes into the bottle, which he takes quickly and settles after.

data_table.Examination: Birth weight 3.42 kg, weight today 3.28 kg, tongue tip notched on protrusion with a thin anterior frenulum, tongue elevates to about half the height of the open mouth, palate intact, no cleft, normal suck on a gloved finger with a shallow latch observed at the breast and the nipple emerging compressed and blanched
data_table.Investigations: Serum bilirubin not indicated, no jaundice

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a frenotomy at this visit and review the weight in one week
options.rationale: Frenotomy relieves nipple pain within days in appropriately selected infants and is a reasonable subsequent step, but around half of infants referred with nipple pain and poor transfer improve with positioning and attachment work alone. Dividing the frenulum before that assessment treats an anatomical finding that may not be the operative cause. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Tongue tie)

options.text: Supply nipple shields and continue direct breastfeeding without other change
options.rationale: Nipple shields can allow feeding to continue through severe trauma and are used under supervision, but they reduce milk transfer if attachment is not corrected and can entrench the shallow latch. Used as a standalone measure in an infant already below birth weight they risk compounding the weight problem. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Breastfeeding support)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Breastfeeding support

options.text: Arrange assessment of positioning and attachment with a lactation consultant
options.rationale: A compressed blanched nipple after feeding with a shallow latch is the signature of an attachment problem, and the fact that he transfers expressed milk quickly and settles shows that suck and swallow are intact and that the limiting step is at the breast. Structured feeding assessment is therefore the intervention that addresses both the pain and the weight, and it also defines whether the frenulum is genuinely restricting function. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Tongue tie)

options.text: Commence formula top ups after each feed and review the weight in one week
options.rationale: Supplementation is indicated when weight loss is severe or when maternal supply is genuinely inadequate, neither of which applies when she is expressing good volumes. Routine formula top ups here would displace breast stimulation and reduce supply while leaving the attachment problem untouched. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Breastfeeding support)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Breastfeeding support

options.text: Refer to an ear nose and throat surgeon for frenuloplasty under anaesthesia
options.rationale: Formal frenuloplasty under general anaesthesia is reserved for a thick posterior or submucosal frenulum, or for revision after a failed simple division, and carries anaesthetic risk in a neonate. This infant has a thin anterior frenulum, which is divided at the bedside without anaesthesia if division is required at all. (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Tongue tie)

explanation.summary: Ankyloglossia is common, present in up to one in ten newborns, and the great majority of affected infants feed without difficulty, so the decision to divide rests on demonstrated functional impairment rather than on the appearance of the frenulum. Assessment covers the mother, including nipple trauma, pain pattern and supply, and the infant, including latch, tongue elevation, milk transfer and weight trajectory. Australian practice is that infants regain birth weight by about fourteen days, and failure to do so triggers a structured feeding review rather than immediate intervention. Frenotomy of a thin anterior frenulum is a bedside procedure with low complication rates and reliable improvement in maternal nipple pain, but published trials show smaller and less certain effects on infant weight gain, and substantial improvement occurs in control groups receiving lactation support alone. Rising rates of division in Australia have prompted advice that lactation assessment precede referral in all but the clearest cases.
key_points: Ankyloglossia occurs in up to ten per cent of newborns and most feed normally
Division is decided on demonstrated function, not on the look of the frenulum
A compressed blanched nipple after feeding indicates a shallow latch
Good transfer of expressed milk shows suck and swallow are intact
Frenotomy improves nipple pain more reliably than it improves infant weight gain
explanation.pearls: Look at the shape of the nipple as it leaves the baby's mouth: a wedge shaped or blanched nipple means compression against the hard palate from a shallow latch and predicts a response to attachment correction, whereas a rounded nipple with continuing pain points to a genuinely restrictive frenulum.

sources.label: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Tongue tie
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Breastfeeding support
RCH CPG: Neonatal weight loss and feeding

subtopic_detail: Months of multifocal bone pain with sterile biopsy and no response to prolonged antistaphylococcal therapy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 10 year old girl in clinic with four months of pain over her right collarbone and her left ankle. The pain wakes her at night and is worse in the mornings, and she has missed sport but not school.

She was admitted three months ago, had a bone biopsy of the clavicle which grew no organisms on extended culture, and completed six weeks of flucloxacillin with no change in her symptoms. She has had no fevers, no weight loss and no night sweats. Her father has psoriasis affecting his elbows.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Firm non fluctuant swelling and tenderness over the medial right clavicle, tenderness over the left distal tibia, no overlying erythema or warmth, no joint effusions, no rash, no nail pitting
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.9 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5), C reactive protein 14 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 32 mm/h (less than 15), blood cultures negative, clavicular biopsy histology shows a mixed inflammatory infiltrate with no organisms on special stains, radiograph of the clavicle shows sclerosis with periosteal new bone

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Whole body magnetic resonance imaging with short tau inversion recovery sequences
options.rationale: Sterile multifocal bone inflammation that has not responded to appropriate antistaphylococcal therapy is chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, and the diagnosis rests on demonstrating additional lesions, many of them clinically silent, at typical sites such as the metaphyses, clavicle, mandible and vertebrae. Whole body imaging without radiation both establishes that multifocal pattern and identifies vertebral involvement that would change management. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis

options.text: Repeat bone biopsy with prolonged culture for mycobacteria and fungi
options.rationale: Repeating the biopsy is what should be done when a single sterile sample is the only evidence against infection, since tuberculous and fungal osteomyelitis can require extended culture. Here the clinical course over four months, a second involved site and complete failure to respond to six weeks of therapy have already made an untreated indolent infection very unlikely. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis

options.text: Technetium bone scan to identify areas of increased osteoblastic activity
options.rationale: Bone scintigraphy also detects multifocal disease and was the traditional test, but it exposes a child to ionising radiation and is markedly less sensitive than magnetic resonance for early marrow oedema and for vertebral lesions. Where whole body magnetic resonance is available it has replaced scintigraphy for this indication. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis

options.text: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine to exclude leukaemia and neuroblastoma
options.rationale: Marrow examination is mandatory when bone pain is accompanied by cytopenias, blasts on film, hepatosplenomegaly or systemic symptoms, since leukaemia presents with bone pain in a substantial minority of children. A normal blood count with normal differential and a preserved general condition over four months argues strongly against it. (Source: RCH CPG: Bone and joint infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bone and joint infection

options.text: Computed tomography of the clavicle to define the extent of bone destruction
options.rationale: Computed tomography characterises cortical destruction and sequestra better than other modalities and is useful when a surgical question exists. It images only the symptomatic site, so it cannot address the multifocality that defines the diagnosis, and it delivers radiation to the thyroid and breast tissue of a 10 year old girl. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis

explanation.summary: Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, also called chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis, is an autoinflammatory bone disease of childhood that mimics infection but has no organism and does not respond to antibiotics. It has a median onset around ten years, affects girls more often, and characteristically involves the metaphyses of long bones, the clavicle, the mandible, the pelvis and the vertebrae. Associations with psoriasis, palmoplantar pustulosis and inflammatory bowel disease in the child or a first degree relative support the diagnosis. It is a diagnosis of exclusion built on a compatible whole body imaging pattern together with sterile histology, and biopsy is directed at excluding infection and malignancy rather than at confirming the condition. First line treatment is a non steroidal anti inflammatory drug, with bisphosphonates or tumour necrosis factor inhibitors for spinal involvement or refractory disease, because untreated vertebral lesions can collapse.
key_points: Sterile bone inflammation unresponsive to antibiotics over months is the presenting pattern
Clavicle, mandible, metaphyses, pelvis and spine are the characteristic sites
Psoriasis or inflammatory bowel disease in the child or a relative supports the diagnosis
Whole body magnetic resonance demonstrates clinically silent additional lesions
Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are first line, with bisphosphonates for spinal disease
explanation.pearls: Look specifically at the vertebrae on whole body imaging: asymptomatic vertebral lesions occur in around a third of children with this condition and are the single finding that escalates treatment from a non steroidal anti inflammatory drug to a bisphosphonate, because vertebra plana from untreated disease is irreversible.

sources.label: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: Chronic non bacterial osteomyelitis
RCH CPG: Bone and joint infection
BMJ Best Practice: Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis

subtopic_detail: Hypoglycaemia during an intercurrent illness with inappropriately low ketones in a toddler who had no newborn screening
stem:
You are the emergency registrar called to a 16 month old boy who has been vomiting and refusing food for 24 hours during a gastroenteritis outbreak at his childcare centre. He was born overseas, arrived in Australia at nine months, and his mother says he had no heel prick test as a newborn.

He is drowsy but rousable and has had no seizure. There is no diarrhoea with blood, no rash and no history of possible ingestion. He has had two similar admissions for drowsiness during viral illnesses in the past year, each time recovering quickly after treatment in another emergency department.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168 per minute, blood pressure 88/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable to voice, capillary refill 3 seconds, liver edge palpable 3 cm below the costal margin, no rash, no focal neurology, pupils equal and reactive
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 1.8 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), blood ketones 0.2 mmol/L (rise above 1.0 with fasting hypoglycaemia), venous pH 7.34 with bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (22-28), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), lactate 1.9 mmol/L (less than 2.0), alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 40)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous glucose now and arrange metabolic testing once he has recovered
options.rationale: Treating the hypoglycaemia first is correct, but the metabolic investigations are interpretable only in the hypoglycaemic state, because acylcarnitines, free fatty acids, insulin, cortisol and urinary organic acids all normalise within hours of glucose. Deferring them converts a diagnosable episode into one that will have to be reproduced by a supervised fast. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Give an intramuscular dose of glucagon and repeat the glucose in fifteen minutes
options.rationale: Glucagon mobilises hepatic glycogen and works in hyperinsulinism, where stores are preserved, but after 24 hours of fasting illness those stores are exhausted and the response will be poor. It also leaves the child hypoglycaemic for longer than intravenous glucose while the diagnostic window closes. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Give oral sucrose by syringe and reassess his conscious state in fifteen minutes
options.rationale: Oral carbohydrate is first line for a hypoglycaemic child who is alert and able to protect the airway, and it is what the family should use at home during future illnesses. A drowsy toddler who has been vomiting for a day cannot be relied upon to absorb or protect, so this route is unsafe here. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Give intravenous hydrocortisone and take a paired cortisol before treatment starts
options.rationale: Adrenal insufficiency does cause hypoglycaemia and a cortisol forms part of the sample set, but it typically comes with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypotension, and the sodium here is 138 mmol/L. Giving hydrocortisone as the single intervention also treats a differential that the ketone result argues against. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Draw the diagnostic blood and urine samples as intravenous glucose is being given
options.rationale: A blood ketone of 0.2 mmol/L alongside a glucose of 1.8 mmol/L is inappropriately low, since a normal child mounts a ketotic response to fasting hypoglycaemia, and that combination with hepatomegaly and transaminitis points to a fatty acid oxidation defect that newborn screening would have caught. The samples that identify it are valid only while the child is hypoglycaemic, so they are collected at the moment intravenous access is obtained rather than delaying the glucose. (Source: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Hypoglycaemia in a child is classified first by the ketone response, because that single result splits the differential in two. A high ketone level indicates the normal fasting response and points to ketotic hypoglycaemia, glycogen storage disease or adrenal insufficiency, whereas a low ketone level in the face of hypoglycaemia is abnormal and points to hyperinsulinism or to a fatty acid oxidation defect, where fat cannot be converted into ketone bodies. Medium chain acyl coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency is the commonest such defect, is detected on the Australian newborn bloodspot screen, and presents in children missed by screening as hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with hepatomegaly and transaminitis during a fasting illness, with a real risk of sudden death. The critical sample, comprising glucose, ketones, insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, free fatty acids, acylcarnitines, ammonia, lactate and the first urine for organic acids, is valid only during hypoglycaemia. Long term management is avoidance of fasting with an emergency regimen of frequent carbohydrate during illness, which converts a potentially fatal condition into a manageable one.
key_points: The ketone level at the time of hypoglycaemia divides the differential in two
Ketones below 1.0 mmol/L during hypoglycaemia are inappropriately low
Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with hepatomegaly suggests a fatty acid oxidation defect
The critical sample is interpretable only while the child is hypoglycaemic
Children who arrive from overseas may have had no newborn bloodspot screening
explanation.pearls: Collect the first urine passed after the hypoglycaemic episode as well as the blood: urinary organic acids showing dicarboxylic aciduria without ketonuria can secure a diagnosis of medium chain acyl coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency even when the blood samples were taken slightly late, and the family can then be given an emergency regimen that prevents sudden death during the next gastroenteritis.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Hypoglycaemia
Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Newborn bloodspot screening
BMJ Best Practice: Inherited disorders of fatty acid oxidation
